frames.note: Start: A joins the queue and is marked as seen.
popleft() takes A from the front. Its neighbours B and C are marked and join the back.
B was first in line, so it goes next. Its new neighbour D is marked and joins the back.
C goes next. Its neighbour D is already marked, so it is not added again.
D goes next. E is marked and joins the queue.
E comes out: that's the goal. Path A → B → D → E, 3 steps. Every cell entered the queue exactly once.
Start: A joins the queue. Nothing is marked yet.
Pop A and mark it. B and C join the queue.
Pop B and mark it. D joins the queue.
Pop C and mark it. D is waiting in the queue but isn't marked yet, so it is added AGAIN.
Pop D and mark it. E joins the queue.
Pop the second copy of D. It's already visited, so it's skipped. That pop was wasted work.
Pop E: goal. The path A → B → D → E is still correct, but the queue held a duplicate. On a big grid that becomes a lot of extra work.
Start at A, distance 0.
Pop A. B and C are 1 step away and join the queue.
Pop B. E is 2 steps away and joins the back, behind C.
Pop C. D is also 2 steps away. Notice that all the 1-step cells were handled before any 2-step cell.
Pop E: goal, after 2 steps via B. Every 1-step cell was already explored, so no shorter route can exist.
Start at A.
Pop A. B and C join the queue.
pop() takes C, the newest item, not B. D joins.
pop() takes D, diving deeper down the same route. E joins.
Pop E: goal found via A → C → D → E, which is 3 steps. But A → B → E is only 2!

steps.title: A queue is a waiting line
steps.body:
Picture a queue at a coffee shop. The first person to join is the first person served: **first in, first out** (FIFO).

BFS puts each cell in this line as soon as it discovers it. Cells discovered earlier are closer to the start, so they are always explored before cells discovered later.

steps.title: Two methods: append() and popleft()
steps.body: `append()` adds to the **back** of the line. `popleft()` removes from the **front**. Used together, things come out in the same order they went in.
steps.code:
from collections import deque

line = deque()
line.append("A")       # A joins the back
line.append("B")       # B joins behind A
first = line.popleft() # "A" leaves from the front
print(first, list(line))  # A ['B']

steps.title: Watch the queue, step by step
steps.body: Here BFS explores a small graph from A to E. New cells join the back and the next cell always comes from the front. Step through it.

steps.title: Common mistake: pop() instead of popleft()
steps.body:
`pop()` removes from the **back**, so the newest cell goes next. The queue becomes a stack and the search turns depth-first: it dives down one route before trying the nearby cells.

It still finds *a* path, just not necessarily the shortest one.

your_code.default: In your code, line {pop_line} takes cells with `popleft()` and line {append_line} adds them with `append()`. Your queue stays first-in, first-out, so the search spreads out one step at a time from the start.
your_code.uses_pop: Your line {pop_line} uses `pop()`, which takes the **newest** cell. That makes your search depth-first. Switching it to `popleft()` restores first-in, first-out order.

alt.title: Another way: ripples in a pond
alt.body: Drop a stone in a pond and the ripple spreads ring by ring. BFS spreads the same way, and the queue is what keeps the rings in order: the inner ring first, then the next one out.

alt.title: Another way: ticket numbers
alt.body: At a deli counter you take a numbered ticket and are served in ticket order. BFS gives each new cell the next ticket and explores cells in ticket order. `popleft()` means "serve the lowest ticket".

checks.prompt: A queue holds `[B, C]`. You call `append("D")` and then `popleft()`. Which cell comes out?

choices.explanation: C is in the middle of the line. `popleft()` always takes the very front, which is B.
Yes. B was first in line, so it's served first.
D just joined the back, so it waits its turn. That's the first-in, first-out rule.

checks.prompt: Why does BFS reach cells 1 step away before cells 2 steps away?

choices.text: It sorts the queue by distance each time
choices.explanation: No sorting happens. FIFO order alone does it: 1-step cells join the line before any 2-step cell is discovered.

choices.text: 1-step cells joined the queue earlier, and the queue serves them first
choices.explanation: Exactly. Discovery order equals distance order, and FIFO preserves it.
A deque only keeps insertion order. That's exactly what BFS needs, but it's not sorting.

checks.prompt: If you replace `popleft()` with `pop()`, what does the search become?

choices.explanation: `pop()` takes the newest item, so the order changes completely.
It runs fine. It just explores in a different order.

choices.text: Depth-first: it dives down the newest route first
choices.explanation: Right. A queue used from the back is a stack, and a stack gives you DFS.

queue_fifo.recap: FIFO order means BFS explores cells in order of how far they are from the start.

steps.title: Chalk marks in a maze
steps.body:
When you explore a maze, you chalk an X on every junction you've found so you don't keep coming back to it. The visited set is that chalk.

The important question is **when** you draw the X: the moment you first *spot* a cell, or only when you get round to *exploring* it?

steps.title: Mark a cell when it joins the queue
steps.body: Here a cell is marked the moment it's appended. From then on, no other neighbour can add it again, so each cell enters the queue **at most once**.

steps.title: Walk through it: marking on append
steps.body: Watch cell D. Both B and C are next to it, but because D is marked as soon as B adds it, C leaves it alone.

steps.title: Common mistake: marking a cell when it leaves the queue
steps.body:
If a cell is only marked when it's popped, another neighbour can add it again while it's still waiting. On a grid most cells have several neighbours, so the queue fills with duplicates and BFS does extra work.

With the goal checked on pop, the path is still a shortest one. The cost is **wasted time and memory**, not a wrong answer.

your_code.default: In your code, lines {visited_lines} handle the visited set. Check that a cell is marked at the moment it's appended (line {append_line}), not later.
your_code.visited_on_dequeue:
Your code marks a cell on line {add_line}, right after popping it on line {pop_line}. The check before appending only sees cells that have already been popped, so a cell still waiting in the queue can be appended again on line {append_line}.

Your path is still shortest. The fix is to call `visited.add(...)` where you append, so each cell is queued once.

alt.title: Simpler: stamp it when you see it
alt.body: Mark a cell the moment you put it in the queue. That's the "I've already got you" stamp. If you wait until you pop it, its other neighbours don't know it's already waiting and add it again.

alt.title: Another way: party invitations
alt.body: You tick a guest's name when you *send* the invite, not when they *arrive*. Otherwise, while you wait for them, someone else might send them a second invite. BFS should tick cells when it queues them.

checks.prompt: Cells B and C are both in the queue, and both are next to D. D is only marked visited when it's popped. After B and C have been popped, how many copies of D are in the queue?

choices.explanation: B adds D. When C is popped, D still isn't marked (it hasn't been popped yet), so C adds it too.
Yes. Nothing marked D while it waited, so both neighbours added it.

choices.text: It depends on which was added last, because the newest comes out first
choices.explanation: That's stack thinking. A BFS queue serves the **oldest** entry first. This builds on FIFO queues.

checks.prompt: In code that marks cells when they're popped (and skips already-visited ones on pop), what is the main cost?

choices.text: Duplicate queue entries and extra work
choices.explanation: Right. The answer is still correct; BFS just does more work than it needs to.
With the goal checked on pop, the first time the goal leaves the queue is still the shortest path. The cost is wasted work.
The skip on pop prevents infinite loops. The duplicates are popped and thrown away.

checks.prompt: Where should `visited.add(nxt)` go so that each cell enters the queue at most once?

choices.explanation: That's the late-marking version: a cell can be appended several times before it's popped.

choices.text: Only when the goal is found
choices.explanation: Then nothing stops cells being revisited at all.
Yes. Mark on append, and no other neighbour can add it again.

visited_set.recap: Mark when you append: each cell joins the queue at most once, so BFS stays O(V + E).

steps.title: Ripples in a pond
steps.body:
Drop a stone in a pond: the ripple reaches everything 1 step away, then 2 steps, then 3. BFS explores the same way.

So the first time it reaches the goal, no shorter route can exist. A shorter route would have reached the goal in an earlier ripple.

steps.title: Each queue entry carries its path
steps.body: Because the queue is FIFO, paths come out **in order of length**: all 1-step paths, then all 2-step paths, and so on. So the first path to reach the goal is a shortest one.

steps.title: Walk through it: distances in order
steps.body: This graph has two routes to E: a 2-step route through B and a 3-step route through C and D. Watch the distances as BFS explores.

steps.title: Common mistake: assuming any search finds the shortest path
steps.body:
Swap the queue for a stack and the search can reach the goal down a long route first.

Also: the guarantee needs **every step to cost the same**. If moves have different costs, you need Dijkstra's algorithm instead.

your_code.default: Your line {goal_line} returns as soon as the goal is popped. Because your queue is first-in, first-out (line {pop_line}), that first pop of the goal comes with a shortest path.

alt.title: Simpler: check everything nearby first
alt.body: BFS checks everything 1 step away, then everything 2 steps away. If the goal turns up while it's checking 2-step cells, there was no 1-step route. If there were, BFS would already have found it.

alt.title: Another way: numbered shelves
alt.body: Imagine books come off a trolley in shelf order 1, 2, 3... The first time you see the goal, you're on the lowest shelf it can possibly be on. BFS's "shelves" are distances.

checks.prompt: BFS pops the goal for the first time with a 4-step path. Could a 3-step path to the goal still be waiting in the queue?

choices.text: Yes, it might be further back
choices.explanation: FIFO order means every 3-step path leaves the queue before any 4-step path.

choices.text: No: all 3-step paths come out before any 4-step path
choices.explanation: Exactly. That's the whole guarantee.

choices.text: Only if the grid has walls
choices.explanation: Walls change which paths exist, not the order they're explored in.

checks.prompt: When does BFS's "first arrival is shortest" guarantee stop holding?

choices.explanation: Walls are fine. Every move still costs one step.

choices.text: When the grid is very large
choices.explanation: Size doesn't matter. Order does.

choices.text: When steps have different costs (a weighted graph)
choices.explanation: Right. With weights, fewest steps isn't the same as cheapest, so you'd use Dijkstra.

checks.prompt: If you swapped the queue for a stack, would the first path found still be shortest?

choices.explanation: Right. A stack dives deep first and can reach the goal down a long route.
A stack serves the newest entry first, so the search dives deep. This builds on FIFO queues.
Even the 5-node example above finds a longer route first with a stack.

shortest_path_guarantee.recap: BFS explores in order of distance, so its first arrival at the goal is a shortest path, as long as every step costs the same.
